Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

vignette: At fifty-eight, Evelyn Hayes stood on the rain-slicked shoulder of Interstate 95, watching paramedics pry open the twisted hood of her husband Arthur’s sedan. The air was thick with the sharp tang of spilled gasoline and scorched upholstery, a sensory imprint that eclipsed any deliberate recollection of the impact. She had been called away to run an errand, and when the dispatcher’s voice fractured with urgency, she rushed to the scene, only to arrive after the final codes were given. The suddenness of the broadside collision, the way Arthur’s car had been struck and spun into the guardrail, left an indelible imprint. She stopped driving, stopped entering the garage, and found that when she tried to deliberately recall the crash, her mind would go strangely blank, as if refusing to hand her the picture she needed. The unbidden return of that sensory memory did not stay contained. When the faint scent of a neighbor’s burning trash drifted through her cracked window, the past flooded her with such visceral clarity that her hands shook. What frightened her most was how something in her surroundings could instantly bring the full memory back without warning, and this involuntary recall directly sharpened her focus on the calendar’s turning days. As the smell lingered, she found herself acutely braced for the approaching anniversary, her attention snapping to the date, and to any siren that might cut through her quiet neighborhood, the memory itself acting as a catalyst that transformed ordinary dates and distant sounds into immediate, unavoidable alarms. Those alarms, once activated, quickly hijacked her physiology. When the annual date of the crash arrived, the mere knowledge of the calendar’s turn sent her pulse racing and her breath shortening. Equally, the low wail of an approaching ambulance down the street would cause her shoulders to hike to her ears and her fingers to tighten around the kitchen counter until her knuckles blanched. Even driving past a wrecker recovering a mangled vehicle would drop her into a state of acute physical alarm, her muscles coiled as if bracing for a fresh impact. The external cues did not merely remind her of Arthur; they forcibly plunged her back into a state of bodily emergency. That physiological surge was fed directly by the memories that would surface without permission. When the olfactory recall struck, transporting her back to the smell of burnt rubber and wet asphalt, her heart would hammer against her ribs so violently that sleep became impossible. She would lie in the dark, eyes wide, counting the minutes past two in the morning, convinced that if she finally dozed, the collision would happen again. The involuntary return of the event’s sensory details directly manufactured the relentless physical tension and sleep disruption that came to define her nights. This exhausted, hypervigilant state, in turn, tightened her focus on the very stimuli she feared. The chronic sleeplessness and constant startle response to any unexpected movement nearby—a falling curtain, a door closing—left her nerves raw and perpetually scanning. Because she was never fully rested or grounded, her attention fixated itself on every possible warning sign. She began tracking the dates with obsessive precision, listening for sirens with trained intensity, and studying every vehicle passing her windows for the telltale signs of a collision. The very state of threat she had cultivated by surviving the aftermath made her increasingly sensitive to, and dependent on, monitoring those same triggers. The house, once a place of shared routines, became a confined perimeter she patrolled alone. Unemployed since Arthur’s death, Evelyn found her days collapsing into a loop of repeatedly checking that doors and windows were locked, and retreating to the living room when the anniversary approached. Her avoidance severed her from the community book club she and Arthur had attended, leaving her isolated in a quiet that felt increasingly suffocating. She came to the clinic because the checking had begun to bleed into daytime, because the anniversary was three weeks away, and because she was finally terrified that her own nervous system had become a permanent guest in her home. She hoped someone could help her sleep, but what she most feared was waking up and realizing the alarm would never truly quiet.
